transcript.content: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hello. Thank you for seeing me. I... I suppose what brings me in is this ongoing situation that I’ve been trying to make sense of for a while now. It started at home, in my apartment. I spend a good deal of time there, and lately I’ve been hearing these voices. And I don't mean muffled sounds like you'd hear from a neighbor's television, I mean very, very clear voices. 

At first, I tried to ignore it, but it's... well, it's women. I can hear them whispering right from behind the walls of my living room. And the thing is, it’s not just happening at my apartment anymore. I went to the museum the other day—I always try to go during the week when it's quiet and the rooms are practically empty so I can really take my time—and I heard them there, too. Right there in the empty museum rooms, the exact same women whispering behind the plaster. 

They are absolutely fixated on this one subject. They keep telling me, very specifically, which photographs belong in the archive. They just whisper back and forth about the archive, sorting through these photographs in their minds, telling me what needs to be categorized and what belongs where. I don't even know which archive they mean, but they go on and on, and it’s just taking up so much of my mental energy trying to follow what they want from me with these pictures. I just can't seem to get them to stop whispering about it.
About how long have you been hearing these voices?

Oh, goodness, let me think. Time has a way of just... well, it slips by, doesn't it? Especially when your days are so completely consumed by something like this. I would have to say it’s been about eight months now. Yes, eight months. I remember because the weather was just starting to change, and I had all the windows shut tight, which is exactly why I knew the sound couldn't possibly be coming from the street or the courtyard. 

At first, I thought, well, maybe it's just the building settling, or the pipes echoing from the floor above, but no. For eight whole months, I've had to listen to these women. And... and it's not just hearing them, Doctor. Over these past eight months, it’s grown into this absolute, undeniable certainty that people are actually watching my archive. They aren't just talking about it blindly, they are actively watching it. I don't know how they manage it through the plaster and the walls, but they are watching the archive and whispering about the photographs, deciding what goes where. 

Eight months of waking up and knowing they are right there, analyzing everything, judging the categorization. It’s a terribly long time to be under that kind of scrutiny, you know? You try to make a simple cup of Earl Grey tea in your own kitchen, and they're whispering. You try to sit quietly in an empty museum to find a moment of peace, and they're watching the archive. Eight months of this constant, relentless... well, it just doesn't stop.
Over these past eight months, have you been feeling persistently down, sad, or hopeless?

Oh, well... no, not really down or sad, no. I mean, I wouldn't use the word hopeless at all. It’s more... well, it's just exhausting, isn't it? But as for feeling sad or down in the dumps, no, I haven't been sitting around crying or feeling sorry for myself, or feeling like there's a big dark cloud over me. I know some people get like that, where they just can't get out of bed or they feel like the whole world is ending, but that hasn't been my experience at all. 

Actually, if anything, I've had to be quite alert. When you have women whispering behind the walls and people watching an archive, you don't really have the luxury of just giving up and feeling hopeless. You have to stay sharp. You have to pay attention to what they're saying about the photographs, even if it doesn't make total sense to you. So no, I wouldn't say I've been depressed or feeling low. It's just... it's a lot of pressure, having all this going on, but it hasn't made me feel sad. Just very, very occupied with trying to understand what they want from the archive. I mean, wouldn't anyone feel a bit overwhelmed if they were in my shoes? But sad? No, definitely not sad.

I am... well, I am just utterly convinced that the museum board—and the city arts people, too, because you know how all these committees are connected, they all go to the same galas and share the same funding—they have been monitoring my phone. It's really the only logical explanation for it. I'll pick up the receiver to make a simple call, even just to check the dial tone, and there's this... this heaviness on the line. I've tried to explain the gravity of this to people, I really have, but... well, no one has shown me anything that proves otherwise. It's all connected to the archive, you see. They just won't let me be.

Oh, heavens no. No, no, no. I mean, well, I might have a small sherry at Christmas, or perhaps a half-glass of champagne if there's a wedding—though honestly, who goes to weddings at my age anymore? But as for drinking regularly, or using drugs? Absolutely not. Never have, never will. 

I just... well, I don't see the appeal, for one thing. And quite frankly, Doctor, I don't think I could afford to dull my senses even if I wanted to. I mean, can you imagine? With the museum board listening in on the telephone and those women whispering behind the plaster, I have to be completely lucid. If I were drinking alcohol, or taking... well, whatever it is people take these days, recreational drugs, marijuana, or those terrible pills you hear about on the news... if I were doing any of that, I'd be completely defenseless. I wouldn't be able to keep the archive safe. They would just swoop in the moment I was incapacitated and take the photographs, and then where would the truth be? It would be locked away in some museum basement, completely suppressed. 

So no, I don't drink. I keep my mind as clear as possible. I drink tea—Earl Grey, mostly, sometimes peppermint if my stomach feels a bit fluttery from all the stress—but nothing stronger. I have to stay vigilant. I have to be ready for whatever the arts council tries next. It's just common sense, really. When you are the sole custodian of a Caribbean archive of this magnitude, you simply cannot afford to have your wits compromised by alcohol or drugs. You just can't.
